content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wings are the small sections of a bird's wing, commonly prepared by frying, baking, or grilling. They are often served with a variety of sauces and seasonings, making them a staple in fast‑food, bar menus, and home cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings became famous in the United States with the invention of "Buffalo wings" in 1964 at the Anchor Bar in Buffalo, New York.
In Japan, chicken wings are popular in teriyaki sauce and topped with toasted sesame seeds.
Common marinades include barbecue, honey‑mustard, garlic, spicy chili, and many regional variations.
In the U.S., wings are traditionally served with celery sticks and blue‑cheese dressing.
Chicken wings contain more protein per 100 g than most other chicken parts, but also more fat when deep‑fried.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Wings provide high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Chicken is a good source of selenium, phosphorus, and zinc, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Moderate iron content
items.content: The iron in chicken is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High fat when fried
items.content: Deep‑fried wings can be calorie‑dense and may contain trans fats if the wrong oil is used.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked wings may harbor salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Sodium in sauces
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain high levels of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

content.title: How to Prepare and Serve
content.content: Marinate wings in soy sauce, honey, garlic, paprika, or hot chili sauce for at least 30 minutes. Then fry in oil, bake at 200 °C for 25‑30 minutes, or grill. Serve hot with blue‑cheese dip, ranch, barbecue sauce, or a yogurt‑based dip, garnished with fresh herbs and lime wedges.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh wings keep in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen wings last up to 9 months at ‑18 °C. Thaw frozen wings in the fridge before cooking, and keep cooked hot wings at room temperature for no more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Creamed corn is a canned product made from mature sweet corn kernels that are cooked in a creamy sauce. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a smooth texture, making it convenient for quick meal preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Creamed corn is a staple side dish in American barbecue and salads.
Canning preserves most of the B‑vitamins, vitamin C, and carotenoids.
The first commercial creamed corn appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
Corn is one of the world’s most produced grain crops, with over 1 billion tonnes harvested annually.
The creamy sauce typically contains butter, milk or cream, and seasonings such as salt and sugar.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Corn provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in corn help protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin, and folate contribute to normal energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in fluid balance and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Creamed corn generally contains less saturated fat than many meat side dishes.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned versions often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: The creamy sauce can include added sugar, increasing the calorie count.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn proteins.

items.title: BPA in packaging
items.content: Metal cans may have trace BPA; choose products in BPA‑free containers when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Creamed corn can be served as a side dish with meat, fish or vegetables, added to salads, soups, pasta, and casseroles. It is also easy to heat in the microwave or on the stovetop with a splash of water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer the corn to a sealed container, refrigerate, and consume within 3‑5 days. Discard if it develops an off odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Gin Fizz is a classic cocktail made with gin, fresh lemon juice, simple syrup and carbonated water. It is light, refreshing and features a bright citrus note highlighted by the juniper-forward gin.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink originated in the early 1920s in the United States as a variation of the popular “fizz” style, which mixes spirit with soda.
The original recipe calls for a simple syrup rather than pre‑made sweetened syrup.
Some versions add egg white, creating a frothy texture often called a “Fizz with foam”.
Gin Fizz is typically served in a highball glass, garnished with a lemon wedge or a sprig of rosemary.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: When consumed in moderation, the cocktail is low in calories because the bulk of the drink is carbonated water.

items.title: Vitamin C from lemon
items.content: Fresh lemon juice provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Digestive boost from gin
items.content: Gin, containing juniper berries, may aid digestion and offers a subtle aromatic effect.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: Like any alcoholic beverage, Gin Fizz can cause intoxication and is not recommended for pregnant individuals, people with liver disease, or those taking certain medications.

items.title: Lemon acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach of people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Gin allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to gin components such as juniper.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: Combine 45 ml gin, 30 ml fresh lemon juice and 15 ml simple syrup in a shaker with ice. Shake well, then strain into a highball glass filled with ice and top with carbonated water. Garnish with a lemon wedge.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ingredients separately: gin in a cool, dark place, lemons in the refrigerator, and use carbonated water shortly after opening.
